decks.title: Organising — Part 1: Meaning, Steps, Importance and Structures
goals: Explain the steps of the organising process and its importance
Recommend a functional or divisional structure for a given business and justify the choice

slides.heading: Organising
slides.body_md: Part 1: what **organising** is, its **steps**, why it **matters**, and the **functional** and **divisional** structures.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the meaning of organising, its steps, its importance, and functional and divisional structures
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A plan says what a firm wants to do. Organising decides who will do which part of the work, with what resources, and who will report to whom. In this part we learn the steps of organising, why it matters, and the two common ways of arranging a firm: by function or by product.

slides.heading: What is organising?
slides.body_md: **Organising** is identifying and grouping the work, assigning it, and setting up authority and reporting relationships so that plans can be carried out.

headers: Imagined example: a fruit canner in Haldwani
rows: Line leaders to shift supervisor to works manager

visual.alt: Table of the four questions organising answers, with an imagined fruit canner's answers

slides.narration: Organising answers four questions. What work must be done? How should it be grouped? Who should do each job? And who reports to whom? Once these are settled, the plan can be turned into action, because everyone knows their task and their place.

slides.heading: Steps in organising

visual.alt: Flow of the four steps of organising: identify and divide the work, departmentalise, assign duties, and establish reporting relationships
visual.caption: Four steps, in order.

slides.narration: First, identify the total work and divide it into jobs. Second, group similar jobs into departments, which is called departmentalisation. Third, assign each job to a person suited to it. Fourth, establish reporting relationships, so that everyone knows whose orders to follow and to whom they answer.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a college food stall
slides.body_md: Students in Kolkata organise a food stall at their college fest.
bullets: Step 1: read each action.
Step 2: match it to a **step of organising**.
Step 3: check the order.

headers: Action for an imagined food stall at a college fest in Kolkata
rows: List jobs: buying, cooking, serving, billing, cleaning
Group them into kitchen and counter teams
Put the best cook in the kitchen and a quick counter in billing
Team leads report to the stall captain

visual.alt: Worked table: four actions for an imagined college food stall matched to the four steps of organising
visual.caption: Each action answers one step, in order.

slides.narration: Listing buying, cooking, serving, billing and cleaning divides the work. Grouping these into kitchen and counter teams is departmentalisation. Putting the best cook in the kitchen assigns duties. Making team leads report to the stall captain establishes reporting relationships.

slides.heading: Quick check: the right person
slides.body_md: A fruit canner appoints a food scientist with laboratory experience to head its new Quality department. Which step of organising is this?
slides.narration: Is this grouping work, or giving it to someone?

slides.heading: Why organising matters

rows: People repeat one kind of job and get better at it
Everyone knows whom to report to
No duplication; no task left undone
Structure can be adjusted for new needs
Clear roles make control and coordination easier
Delegation lets people learn and grow
New units fit into a clear structure

visual.alt: Table of seven points of importance of organising with a short explanation of each

slides.narration: Organising brings seven benefits. People specialise and improve. Working relationships become clear. Resources are used fully, without duplication. The firm can adapt to change. Administration becomes effective. People develop through delegation. And the firm can expand, because new units fit into a clear structure.

slides.heading: Quick check: is reporting part of it?
slides.body_md: True or false: organising is complete once jobs are grouped into departments; deciding who reports to whom is not part of it.
slides.narration: Count the steps of organising.

visual.caption: Divisional structure: divisions by product.

slides.narration: In a divisional structure, each product line becomes a division with its own production, sales and accounts. It suits a firm with several very different products. Each division can be judged on its own profit, and its head gains all-round skills. But functions are duplicated, so it costs more.

slides.heading: Functional or divisional?
columns:
**Functional**

One main product; specialists by function; economical.

**Divisional**

Several products; a profit centre for each; costlier.

visual.alt: Table comparing functional and divisional structures on grouping, suitability, specialisation, cost, accountability and main risk

slides.narration: To compare them, look at grouping, suitability, specialisation, cost and accountability. Functional groups by function, suits one product, and is economical, but results are hard to pin on anyone. Divisional groups by product, suits many products, and makes each division answer for its profit, but it duplicates functions.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: which structure?
slides.body_md: Recommend a structure for three imagined firms.
bullets: Step 1: ask **one product or several?**
Step 2: check whether products need **different methods and markets**.
Step 3: recommend and give a reason.

rows: A mill making only sago on a large scale
A group making dairy, furniture and bags
A rice mill that adds cattle feed and furniture
New lines need their own units

visual.alt: Worked table recommending a functional or divisional structure for three imagined firms, with reasons
visual.caption: Ask: one product, or several very different ones?

slides.narration: A mill that makes only sago on a large scale should be functional: one product, with specialists for each function. A group making dairy, furniture and bags should be divisional, because its products are very different. A rice mill that adds cattle feed and furniture should also move to divisions.

slides.heading: Quick check: an analogy
slides.body_md: Complete the analogy: purchase, production and sales departments are to functional structure as dairy, furniture and travel-bag units are to ___ structure.
slides.narration: Are these units built around functions, or around products?

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Grouping work, assigning it and fixing reporting lines
Specialisation, clarity, resources, change, administration, people, growth
Functional for one product; divisional for several

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: meaning, steps and importance of organising, and the two structures

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Organising groups work, assigns it and fixes reporting lines. Its four steps are dividing work, departmentalising, assigning duties and establishing reporting relationships. It brings specialisation, clarity and growth. A functional structure suits one main product; a divisional structure suits several different products.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Learn the **four steps in order**.
For structure questions, ask **one product or several**.
Duplication is a limit of **divisional**; inter-department conflict is a limit of **functional**.
Always give a **reason** with a recommendation.

visual.alt: Three steps for case questions: quote the line, name the concept, and explain the link

slides.narration: A few tips. Learn the four steps in order. When recommending a structure, first ask whether the firm has one product or several. Remember that duplication belongs to the divisional structure and conflict between departments to the functional one. And always back a recommendation with a reason.

decks.title: Organising — Part 2: Formal and Informal Organisation, Delegation and Decentralisation
goals: Distinguish formal from informal organisation and explain how each affects work
Explain the elements of delegation and its importance
Compare centralisation and decentralisation, and distinguish delegation from decentralisation

slides.heading: Formal, Informal, Delegation and Decentralisation
slides.body_md: Part 2: **formal** and **informal** organisation, **delegation** of authority, and **centralisation** and **decentralisation**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: formal and informal organisation, delegation of authority, and centralisation and decentralisation
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Every firm has two organisations: the one on the chart and the one that grows among people. In this part we compare them, then see how managers pass authority down through delegation, and how far a firm should spread decision making through decentralisation.

slides.heading: Formal organisation
slides.body_md: **Formal organisation** is the structure of jobs and authority deliberately designed by management.

rows: Structure of jobs and authority deliberately designed by management
Written duties; official chart; follows the scalar chain
Easy to fix responsibility; avoids duplication; gives stability
Delays; ignores social needs; discourages initiative

visual.alt: Table of the meaning, features, merits and limits of formal organisation

slides.narration: Formal organisation is the planned structure. It has written duties, an official chart, and communication through the scalar chain. It makes responsibility easy to fix, avoids duplication and gives stability. But it can be slow, it ignores people's social needs, and it may discourage initiative.

slides.heading: Informal organisation
slides.body_md: **Informal organisation** is the network of relationships that grows naturally from social interaction at work.

rows: Network of relationships that grows from social interaction
Not planned; not on the chart; communicates through the grapevine
Fast communication; meets social needs; fills gaps in rules
Rumours; may resist change; group pressure

visual.alt: Table of the meaning, features, merits and limits of informal organisation

slides.narration: Informal organisation grows on its own, from friendships and shared interests. It does not appear on any chart, and news travels through the grapevine. It is fast, it meets social needs and it fills gaps in the rules. But it can spread rumours, resist change and press members to conform.

slides.heading: Formal versus informal
columns:
**Formal**

Designed by management; on the chart; scalar chain.

**Informal**

Grows on its own; not on the chart; grapevine.

visual.alt: Table comparing formal and informal organisation on origin, purpose, communication, whether shown on the chart, and nature

slides.narration: Compare the two on origin, purpose and communication. Formal organisation is created by management for organisational goals and works through the scalar chain. Informal organisation arises on its own to meet social needs, and its communication runs in any direction. Wise managers use both.

slides.heading: Quick check: an analogy
slides.body_md: Complete the analogy: the official chart of positions is to formal organisation as friendship groups that grow on their own are to ___ organisation.
slides.narration: Was the friendship group designed by management?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: formal or informal?
slides.body_md: Sort four imagined facts from an engineering works in Bokaro.
bullets: Step 1: ask whether it was **designed by management**.
Step 2: if not, it is **informal**.
Step 3: name any special feature, such as the grapevine.

headers: Imagined fact at an engineering works in Bokaro
rows: Written job description for every post
Fitters who share a bus swap machine tips
Tool requests go through supervisor and shop manager
News of a bonus spreads in an hour

visual.alt: Worked table classifying four imagined facts at an engineering works as formal or informal organisation
visual.caption: Ask: was it designed by management, or did it grow on its own?

slides.narration: Written job descriptions are designed by management, so they are formal. Fitters who swap tips on the bus form an informal group. Tool requests that pass through the supervisor follow the formal chain. A bonus rumour spreading in an hour is the grapevine, which is informal.

slides.heading: Delegation and its three elements
slides.body_md: **Delegation** is passing authority to a subordinate to carry out a task, while the manager remains answerable for the result.

rows: Obligation to do the task well

visual.alt: Table of the three elements of delegation, responsibility, authority and accountability, with meaning, direction and whether each can be delegated

slides.narration: Delegation has three elements. Responsibility is the subordinate's duty to do the task well. Authority is the right to decide and give orders, and it flows downward. Accountability is being answerable for the result. It flows upward, and it cannot be delegated: the manager still answers to her own boss.

slides.heading: Why delegate?

rows: An owner hands over daily ice orders and meets export buyers
A cashier learns to approve refunds
Clear authority shows who handles what
New managers are ready when outlets open

visual.alt: Table of five points of importance of delegation, each with an imagined example

slides.narration: Delegation frees managers from routine work so they can focus on important matters. It develops employees by giving them real decisions. It motivates them, because being trusted feels good. It improves coordination, since everyone knows who handles what. And it prepares managers for growth.

slides.heading: Quick check: which way it flows
slides.body_md: True or false: authority flows downward from superior to subordinate, while accountability flows upward.
slides.narration: Who gives the right to decide, and who answers for the result?

slides.heading: Centralisation and decentralisation
columns:
**Decentralisation**

Authority spread systematically to all levels, within limits.

visual.alt: Table comparing centralisation and decentralisation on where decisions are taken, speed, suitability and effect on managers below

slides.narration: Centralisation keeps decision making at the top. It suits small firms and key policy matters, but it slows a large firm down. Decentralisation spreads authority to lower levels, allowing quick local decisions and developing managers. No firm is fully one or the other; the best is a balance that suits its size and spread.

slides.heading: Delegation versus decentralisation

rows: Between a superior and a subordinate
To give more freedom to lower levels

visual.alt: Table comparing delegation and decentralisation on nature, scope, purpose and freedom

slides.narration: Delegation and decentralisation are linked but different. Delegation is compulsory, because no manager can do everything alone, and it happens between a superior and a subordinate. Decentralisation is an optional policy of top management that spreads authority across all levels. It is delegation extended throughout the organisation.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: who decides?
slides.body_md: Four imagined facts from a turmeric trader in Erode.
bullets: Step 1: ask **who** decides.
Step 2: ask **at how many levels**.
Step 3: name the concept.

headers: Imagined fact at a turmeric trader in Erode
rows: Owner alone decided prices and hiring, before depots
Depots fix buying prices within limits
A supervisor lets a clerk sign delivery notes
Head office keeps export pricing and loans

visual.alt: Worked table matching four imagined facts at a turmeric trader with centralisation, decentralisation, delegation, and key decisions kept central
visual.caption: Ask: who decides, and at how many levels?

slides.narration: When the owner alone decided prices and hiring, that was centralisation. Now that depots fix buying prices within limits, authority is decentralised. A supervisor letting a clerk sign delivery notes is delegation. Keeping export pricing and loans at head office shows that key decisions stay central, giving a balance.

slides.heading: Quick check: four depots
slides.body_md: Each regional depot fixes its own buying prices and hires its own loaders, within limits set by head office. What does this show?
slides.narration: Is authority kept at the top, or spread across levels?

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: Designed by management vs grows on its own
Decisions at the top vs spread across levels; balance is best

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: formal and informal organisation, elements of delegation, accountability, and centralisation versus decentralisation

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. Formal organisation is designed by management; informal organisation grows on its own, and both affect work. Delegation passes responsibility and authority down, while accountability stays with the manager. Centralisation keeps decisions at the top; decentralisation spreads them. A balance usually works best.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: **Accountability cannot be delegated**; say so whenever delegation appears.
Delegation is **compulsory**; decentralisation is **optional**.
Grapevine and rumours point to **informal** organisation.
For centralisation questions, end with a **balanced verdict**.

visual.alt: Three steps for case questions: quote the line, name the concept, and explain the link

slides.narration: Final tips. Whenever delegation appears, mention that accountability cannot be delegated. Remember that delegation is compulsory while decentralisation is optional. Rumours and the grapevine signal informal organisation. And in centralisation questions, end with a balanced verdict on what to keep at the top.

sections.heading: 2. Functional and divisional structures
sections.body_md:
**Functional structure:** activities grouped by major function (purchase, production, finance, sales), each under a specialist. **Suits** a large firm with one main product. **Merits:** specialisation; economy, since functions are not duplicated; easy control within each function. **Demerits:** departments may put their own goals first and conflict; it is hard to fix responsibility for overall results; it gives managers narrow experience.

**Divisional structure:** activities grouped by product line, each division having its own functions. **Suits** a firm with several different products. **Merits:** each division is a profit centre, so results are measurable; division heads gain all-round skills; new products can be added easily. **Demerits:** duplication of resources raises cost; divisions may compete for funds.

key_terms.definition_md: Grouping by product line, each division with its own functions.
A unit whose own profit can be measured.

sections.heading: 3. Formal and informal organisation
sections.body_md:
**Formal organisation:** the structure deliberately designed by management, with written duties, an official chart and communication through the scalar chain. **Merits:** responsibility is easy to fix; duplication is avoided; it gives stability. **Limits:** delays; it ignores social needs; it may discourage initiative.

**Informal organisation:** the network of relationships that arises from social interaction, not planned by management and not on the chart; communication flows through the **grapevine**. **Merits:** fast communication; meets social needs; fills gaps in the formal system; managers can sense feelings. **Limits:** rumours; resistance to change; pressure to conform.

sections.heading: 4. Delegation of authority
sections.body_md:
**Delegation** is the passing of authority by a superior to a subordinate to carry out an assigned task, while the superior stays answerable for the result.

**Elements:**
- **Responsibility** — the subordinate's obligation to do the task properly; it arises from the superior–subordinate relationship.
- **Authority** — the right to take decisions and give orders; it flows downward and should match responsibility.
- **Accountability** — answerability for the result; it flows upward and **cannot be delegated**.

**Importance:** effective management (managers are freed for important work); employee development; motivation; better coordination; a basis for growth and for the management hierarchy.

sections.heading: 5. Centralisation and decentralisation
sections.body_md:
**Centralisation:** decision-making authority is kept at the top. Suits small firms and key policy matters; slows decisions in large firms; gives lower managers little chance to learn.

**Decentralisation:** authority is spread systematically to lower levels, within limits. **Merits:** quick local decisions; develops managers; relieves top management; allows better control through measurable units. Complete decentralisation is not desirable: key decisions such as overall policy and finance stay central. A **balance** is best.

**Delegation vs decentralisation:** delegation is compulsory, narrow (superior to subordinate) and done to lighten a manager's load; decentralisation is an optional policy, wide (all levels) and done to give lower levels more freedom. Decentralisation is delegation extended throughout the organisation.

questions.stem_md: The founder of the imagined Haldwani Fruit Canners begins organising by listing every job the business needs — washing, peeling, cooking, canning, labelling and selling — and splitting them into tasks one person can handle. Which step of organising is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Identification and division of work. Listing the total work and breaking it into manageable jobs is identification and division of work, the first step of organising.

questions.stem_md: At the imagined Haldwani Fruit Canners, cooking, canning and labelling jobs are placed under a Production unit, while advertising and dealer visits go to a Marketing unit. This step is called
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** departmentalisation. Grouping similar or related jobs into units or departments is departmentalisation.

questions.stem_md: The works manager of the imagined Haldwani Fruit Canners announces that each line leader will report to the shift supervisor, who will report to her. Which step of organising is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Establishing reporting relationships. Deciding who reports to whom creates the chain of authority: establishing reporting relationships.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Assignment of duties. Giving each job to the person best suited to it by skill and experience is assignment of duties.

questions.stem_md: Because its jobs, departments and reporting lines were clearly set out, the imagined Salem Sago Mills was able to add a second mill with sixty more workers without confusion. Which importance of organising does this show?

It removes the need for managers
It helps in expansion and growth

List all the work: stalls, tickets, publicity, cleaning, security
Give each team to members with suitable skills

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (c) → (a) → (d) → (b). Identification and division of work, departmentalisation, assignment of duties, and establishing reporting relationships.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Organising helps in the best possible use of resources.

**Reason (R):** A clear division of work avoids duplication and makes sure no task is left undone.

Choose the correct option.

Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and the reason explains the assertion: when work is clearly divided, people, money and materials are not wasted on duplicated or forgotten tasks.

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Establishing reporting relationships is the last step of organising; without it, no one knows whom to answer to.

questions.stem_md: An imagined school in Bhubaneswar is organising its sports day. Explain the first two steps of organising with an example of each from the event.
questions.solution_md: Both steps explained with sports-day examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Identification and division of work:** list every job, such as **marking tracks, timing races, first aid and prize giving**, and split it into tasks.
2. **Departmentalisation:** **group** related jobs into teams, such as a **track team** and a **welfare team**.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Sundargarh Steel Furniture has grown from 30 to 300 workers in four years. Explain three ways in which sound organising will help it now.
questions.solution_md: Three points of importance applied to the growing firm.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Benefits of specialisation:** welders, painters and fitters each do **one kind of job** repeatedly, so skill and speed improve.
2. **Clarity in working relationships:** everyone knows **whom to report to**, which reduces confusion and fixes responsibility.
3. **Adaptation to change:** a clear structure lets the firm **add new lines**, such as hospital beds, by adjusting departments rather than starting afresh.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Kota Doria Weavers' Cooperative has listed all the work needed to open its first showroom. Explain the next three steps of organising it should follow, with an example of each.
questions.solution_md: The three later steps applied to the showroom.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Departmentalisation:** group the jobs into units such as **display and sales**, **stock and accounts**, and **publicity**.
2. **Assignment of duties:** give each unit to suitable members, for example the **best talker to sales** and the member who keeps accounts to stock.
3. **Establishing reporting relationships:** decide that unit heads **report to the showroom manager**, who reports to the cooperative's committee.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is meant by organising? [1]
(b) Ananya is setting up an imagined music school in Guwahati with eight teachers and four office staff. Explain the four steps of organising she should follow, with an example of each. [4]
questions.solution_md: Meaning; the four steps applied to the music school.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Organising** is the process of **identifying and grouping work**, assigning it to people, and establishing **authority and reporting relationships** so that plans can be carried out.

(b) 1. **Identification and division of work:** list all the work, such as **teaching, admissions, fee collection, concerts** and upkeep, and divide it into jobs.
2. **Departmentalisation:** group related jobs into units, such as **teaching** (by instrument) and **administration**.
3. **Assignment of duties:** give each job to a suitable person, for example the **senior sitar teacher** heads the string section.
4. **Establishing reporting relationships:** teachers report to their **section head**, and section heads and the office manager report to **Ananya**.

answer.model_answer_md:

1. **Different products:** rice, cattle feed and furniture need **different production methods and markets**, so each should have its own division.
2. **Accountability:** each division's **profit or loss** can be measured, so poor performers are spotted.

questions.stem_md:
The imagined Bhagalpur Silk House now makes silk saris, silk cushion covers and runs a silk-village homestay for tourists.
(a) Which organisation structure would you recommend for it? Give one reason. [1]
(b) Distinguish between functional and divisional structures on four bases. [4]
questions.solution_md: A recommendation with a reason; four bases of difference.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A **divisional structure**, because its three lines — saris, cushion covers and tourism — need **different skills and markets**.

(b) 1. **Basis of grouping:** functional groups activities by **major function** (purchase, production, sales); divisional groups them by **product line**.
2. **Specialisation:** functional gives **functional** specialisation; divisional gives **product** specialisation, and managers gain all-round skills.
3. **Cost:** functional is **economical** because functions are not duplicated; divisional is **costlier** because each division repeats functions.
4. **Suitability and accountability:** functional suits a firm with **one main product**, and it is hard to fix responsibility for results; divisional suits **several product lines**, and each division answers for its own profit.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined bank branch in Thrissur, clerks who belong to the same choir often settle small problems over tea instead of waiting for official meetings. Identify the type of organisation and state one benefit and one risk of it.
questions.solution_md: Type identified with one benefit and one risk.

answer.model_answer_md: **Informal organisation.** **Benefit:** problems are solved **faster** and staff feel a sense of belonging. **Risk:** the group may spread **rumours** or resist decisions it dislikes.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between formal and informal organisation on three bases: origin, purpose and flow of communication.
questions.solution_md: Three bases of difference.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Origin:** formal organisation is **deliberately created by management**; informal organisation **arises on its own** from social interaction.
2. **Purpose:** formal aims at **organisational goals**; informal meets members' **social and personal needs**.
3. **Flow of communication:** formal communication follows the **scalar chain**; informal communication moves **in any direction**, often through the grapevine.

questions.stem_md: Explain three ways in which the informal organisation at the imagined Gwalior Stone Carvers could help its management.
questions.solution_md: Three benefits applied to the firm.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Faster communication:** news travels quickly through the **grapevine**, so urgent messages reach everyone fast.
2. **Meets social needs:** groups such as the **chess club** give carvers a sense of belonging, raising morale and reducing turnover.
3. **Fills gaps in the formal structure:** experienced carvers **help newcomers** and solve problems that written rules do not cover, and managers can sense workers' feelings through these groups.

questions.stem_md:

**Reason (R):** A person cannot be expected to complete a task without the power to take the decisions it needs.

Choose the correct option.

Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and the reason explains the assertion: responsibility without matching authority makes the task impossible to complete.

questions.stem_md: In delegation, authority flows downward from superior to subordinate, while accountability flows upward from subordinate to superior.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. The superior passes authority down; the subordinate answers upward for how it was used.

questions.stem_md: Explain authority and accountability as elements of delegation.
questions.solution_md: Both elements explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Authority:** the **right to take decisions** and give orders within a defined area; it **flows downward** and should match the responsibility given.
2. **Accountability:** being **answerable** to the superior for the result of the task; it **flows upward** and **cannot be delegated**.

questions.stem_md: The owner of the imagined Karwar Fisheries has begun delegating authority to her three supervisors. Explain three benefits she and the firm can expect.
questions.solution_md: Three benefits of delegation applied to the firm.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Effective management:** freed from **routine orders**, the owner can focus on export buyers and new markets.
2. **Employee development:** supervisors learn to **take decisions**, building skills for higher posts.
3. **Motivation and better coordination:** trust and authority **raise supervisors' morale**, and clear authority, responsibility and accountability show who handles what, so work moves smoothly.

questions.stem_md:
The owner of the imagined Udupi Tiffin Rooms tells her new manager, Divya: "You will run the evening shift. You may hire part-time servers and buy vegetables up to a weekly limit. Each Monday, report to me on sales and complaints."
(a) Identify the three elements of delegation in these instructions and explain each. [3]
(b) Explain two ways in which this delegation is important for the restaurant. [2]
questions.solution_md: Three elements identified from the instructions; two points of importance.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) 1. **Responsibility:** "**You will run the evening shift**" — Divya is **obliged** to carry out this task properly.
2. **Authority:** "**hire part-time servers and buy vegetables up to a weekly limit**" — she has the **right to decide** within these limits.
3. **Accountability:** "**report to me on sales and complaints**" — she is **answerable** to the owner for the results, though the owner stays answerable to the partners.

(b) 1. **Frees the owner:** she can spend time on **new outlets** and suppliers instead of running every shift.
2. **Develops and motivates Divya:** taking real decisions builds her **skills and confidence**, preparing her for higher posts.

questions.stem_md:
A student at an imagined school in Ujjain writes four statements:
P. Delegation is compulsory in any organisation where a manager cannot do all the work alone.
Q. Decentralisation is an optional policy decision of top management.
R. Delegation and decentralisation have exactly the same scope.
S. Decentralisation extends delegation to the lowest levels of the organisation.
Which statements are correct?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** P, Q and S. P, Q and S are correct. R is wrong: delegation is between a superior and a subordinate, while decentralisation spreads authority across the whole organisation, so its scope is wider.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Decentralisation is an optional policy decision of top management.

**Reason (R):** Decentralisation means delegating authority only to the managing director.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The assertion is true. The reason is false: decentralisation spreads authority systematically to all levels, down to the lowest, not just to one person.

questions.stem_md: Under decentralisation, top management gives away all its authority and keeps none.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Top management keeps authority over major decisions such as overall policy and coordination; complete decentralisation is neither possible nor desirable.

questions.stem_md: Complete the analogy. Delegation : compulsory :: Decentralisation : ___
questions.solution_md: Delegation is compulsory, since no manager can do all the work alone; decentralisation is an optional policy decision of top management.

questions.stem_md: Match each situation at the imagined Erode Turmeric Traders with the concept it shows.

options.text_md: Before the depots were set up, the owner alone decided all prices and hiring
Depots now fix buying prices within limits set by head office
A depot supervisor lets a clerk sign delivery notes
The supervisor still answers to the depot head for any errors in those notes

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). All decisions at the top is centralisation; authority spread to depots is decentralisation; passing one task down is delegation; remaining answerable is accountability.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between delegation and decentralisation on two bases.
questions.solution_md: Two valid bases (nature, scope, freedom of action, status, purpose).

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Nature:** delegation is **compulsory**, since no manager can do all the work alone; decentralisation is an **optional policy decision** of top management.
2. **Scope:** delegation is **narrow**, between a superior and a subordinate; decentralisation is **wide**, spreading authority across **all levels**.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Erode Turmeric Traders has given its four regional depots the authority to fix buying prices and hire staff. Explain three benefits it can expect from decentralisation.
questions.solution_md: Three benefits applied to the trader.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Quicker decisions:** depot heads can **respond at once** to local crop prices without waiting for head office.
2. **Develops managers:** depot heads gain **experience in decision making**, preparing them for top posts.
3. **Relief to top management and better control:** head office is freed to focus on **exports and strategy**, and each depot's results can be **measured** separately.

questions.stem_md: The managing director of the imagined Siliguri Tea Traders, which now has ten branches, still decides everything himself. Evaluate whether this complete centralisation suits the firm, giving three points.
questions.solution_md: Three points leading to a balanced verdict.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Delays:** branches must **wait for his approval** on small matters, so customers and chances are lost.
2. **Overload and weak managers:** he is **overburdened**, and branch heads never learn to take decisions, so the firm has no **successors**.
3. **Some central control is still needed:** overall **pricing policy** and finance should stay with him. **Verdict:** complete centralisation does **not** suit a ten-branch firm; it should decentralise routine decisions and keep key ones central.

questions.stem_md:
The imagined Siliguri Tea Traders, with ten branches across north Bengal and Sikkim, is losing customers because branch managers must ask head office before every small decision.
(a) Distinguish between centralisation and decentralisation on two bases. [2]
(b) Evaluate whether the firm should decentralise, and say what authority it should keep at the centre. [3]
questions.solution_md: Two bases of difference; a reasoned verdict for decentralisation with what to keep central.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) 1. **Meaning:** centralisation **keeps decision-making authority at the top**; decentralisation **spreads it systematically** to lower levels.
2. **Speed and suitability:** centralisation suits **small** firms but slows decisions as a firm grows; decentralisation allows **quick local decisions** in large, spread-out firms.

(b) **Yes, it should decentralise.** Branch managers know **local buyers** and can act at once on prices, stock and staff, so customers will not be lost to delay. They will also **gain experience** and become future leaders, and head office will be freed for **strategy**.
**Keep at the centre:** overall **pricing policy**, major **investments**, the **brand** and finance, so that branches stay coordinated. A **balance** between the two is best.
